items.card: NOTE
items.text:
Effective reading, summarizing, and building a POV

As you begin your journey at Mesa, one of the most important shifts you will experience is not just the volume of content, but the way you are expected to engage with it.

In a startup environment, reading is not a passive activity. Founders and operators are constantly learning through articles, reports, case studies, and market insights. Whether it is understanding a new sector, analyzing a competitor, or spotting an emerging trend, your ability to read and make sense of information directly impacts the quality of your decisions.

This means the goal is not to read more. The goal is to read better.

Objectives

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Identify key ideas, arguments, and insights in business articles and startup content

Summarise complex information clearly in your own words

Form and articulate an evidence-based opinion, distinguishing fact from interpretation

Read with intent as a founder, not just as a student

Build a system to retain, connect, and apply what you learn

Think about the last business article or report you came across. Did you read it end-to-end, or skim through it? Did you question the author’s assumptions, or accept them at face value? Did you connect it to anything you already knew?

Take a moment to reflect:

What is one thing you already do when reading?

What is one challenge you face?

It could be something like getting lost in details, struggling to identify bias, or forgetting what you read soon after. These are common, and this module is designed to help you move past them.

To set the stage, please watch/read the following:

Video (5 min): “Speed Reading Harvard Business Review – How to Read Business Cases Faster” – Paul Nowak (Iris Reading). (A quick demonstration of efficient reading strategies for dense business texts.)

Short Article: “The Art of Summarizing in Business: When, Where, and Why It Matters.” This article highlights why being able to distil complex reports into brief summaries is a valued skill in management


Key takeaway: Effective summarization shows respect for your audience’s time and proves you truly grasp the material. In fast-paced MBA classes and meetings, concise communication = credibility.

(Choose either the video or the article to start, or both if you’re curious. They illustrate why we need strong reading & summarising skills in business.)

Strategies for reading and forming opinions:

Now let’s build your toolkit for reading and summarising effectively. We’ll cover skimming, deep reading, note-taking, and opinion-forming. Start with this brief resource:

Article (8 min read): “Reading Strategies: Skimming and Scanning Techniques.” – Focus on the Skimming section for how to get the gist of an article quickly​.
Key points:

Read the title, headings, and any summary/abstract first.

Read the introductory paragraph and the first and last sentences of each paragraph​

Note bold or italicized terms (they often signal important concepts).

If something is confusing or seems important, pause and read that part fully

Skimming is great for previewing a text or reviewing it before meetings​.

A few tips & examples:

Here are some best practices to guide your reading and summarising, as described in these two articles

    Active and Critical Reading

    Summary vs Analysis

Active Reading: Don’t read passively; engage with the text. For example, make brief notes or highlights as you read – underline key sentences, jot margin notes, or use a digital highlighter. This keeps you focused and helps retention​
(Tip: try writing a one-line summary of each section or page in your own words as you go.)

Separate Facts from Opinions: As you read a business article, ask: What is the author’s thesis or main claim? What evidence is provided? Good readers constantly evaluate if the evidence is objective and credible​. Is the author trying to convince me of something? Recognize bias or assumptions by questions like: “Is the writer’s argument logical or is it based on a faulty assumption?”​

Summarizing Technique – PARAPHRASE: When you summarize, always use your own words. A summary is not copying sentences. It’s conveying the author’s ideas concisely, in a new way. This shows you truly understand the material​.

(Example: Original text: “Executives observe a drop in productivity in remote teams due to reduced in-person collaboration.” → Summary: “According to the article, working remotely can hurt productivity because people collaborate less face-to-face.”)

Forming an Opinion: After understanding the text, form your stance. Ask yourself: Do I agree with the author’s conclusions? Why or why not? Your opinion should be evidence-based – meaning it refers back to facts or points from the reading​​.

For example, if an article argues that “AI will revolutionize finance” and you’re not convinced, your opinion could be: “I’m sceptical about the claim that AI alone will revolutionise finance because the author provided only one case study of success. We need broader evidence. However, I do agree AI can streamline certain tasks (as the article’s statistics on cost savings showed).” – Here you’re citing the article’s evidence (or lack thereof) to justify your stance.

(Feel free to refer to the resource links as you digest these tips. They illustrate concepts like skimming, annotating, etc., in more detail.)

How to read and ensure you retain

One of the biggest challenges with learning at this level is retention.

You will be exposed to a large number of ideas, but without a system, most of them will fade quickly. The goal is to create a way to revisit, connect, and build on what you learn over time.

This is where tools like NotebookLM can play a role.

Instead of treating each article or lecture as a separate experience, you can bring your materials together and interact with them. You can ask questions, generate summaries, compare ideas across sources, and revisit information in different formats.

The value here is the ability to move from consuming information to synthesizing it. Over time, this helps you see patterns, identify contradictions, and develop a deeper understanding of the space you are exploring.

Play Video

Note-taking as a thinking system

If reading is the input, note-taking determines what stays with you.

Most note-taking is focused on capturing information. While this is useful, it is not enough. To truly learn, your notes need to evolve into a system that helps you think.

A helpful way to approach this is to think in layers.

The first layer is simply capturing what happened, whether it is a lecture, a discussion, or an article. The second layer is synthesis, where you identify what actually mattered. The third layer is interpretation, where you reflect on what it means and how it connects to your thinking.

Tools like Granola can support the first two layers by recording, transcribing, and organizing information. This allows you to stay present during discussions instead of trying to capture everything manually.

However, the third layer is where real learning happens. This is where you question, connect, and build your own perspective.

Over time, as you revisit your notes and combine them with new inputs, isolated pieces of information begin to form a coherent understanding.

Bringing it together

What you are building through this process is a system for learning as a founder.

AI can help you manage scale, organize content, and reduce repetitive effort. But the real value comes from how you use that support to think better.

Your role is to decide what matters, connect ideas across domains, and form clear, independent judgments.

In a startup environment, this ability compounds quickly. The better you get at learning from the world around you, the better you become at navigating uncertainty, spotting opportunities, and making decisions.

Before we wrap up, try reading the Indus valley Annual Report attached herein and see for yourself the progress you’ve made in dealing with your reading and synthesising.

items.text:
Activity
Step 1: Read with intent

Read the article: Twelve ‘why not’, ‘post-agentic AI’ Indian e-commerce scenarios from 2028

As you begin, avoid going line by line immediately. First, scan the structure. Notice how the article is organized into scenarios. Pay attention to the central theme of AI agents and how they interact with platforms, users, and businesses.

Then read in detail. As you go, try to identify patterns across scenarios rather than treating each one in isolation. 

Step 2: Identify the core Idea

Once you’ve read the piece, pause and ask yourself:

What is the central argument or thesis of this article?

What is changing in the ecosystem because of AI agents?

Which assumptions about current startups or platforms are being challenged?

Focus on understanding the big shift, not just the individual examples. 

Step 3: Synthesize the scenarios

Instead of summarizing all 12 scenarios, distill them.

Write a short summary in 4 to 5 sentences that answers:

What kind of future is the author imagining?

What happens to aggregators, marketplaces, and platforms in this world?

What role do AI agents play in decision-making and transactions?

Think of this as explaining the article to someone who has not read it.

Step 4: Form Your perspective

Now move beyond the article.

In 2 to 3 sentences, respond to the following:

Which one scenario felt most realistic or interesting to you, and why?

Do you agree with the direction the article suggests?

If you were building a startup today, how would this change your approach?

This is where you move from understanding to judgment.

Step 5: Think like a founder

Take one layer deeper.

Reflect briefly:

In a world where AI agents reduce discovery and comparison to zero, where does value shift?

What kind of startups become stronger? Which ones become fragile?

You do not need perfect answers. The goal is to start asking better questions.

Submission

Post the following in the WhatsApp group:

Your 4 to 5 sentence summary

Your perspective (2 to 3 sentences)

One insight or question that stayed with you after reading

Startup Awareness

"Did you know that 3 new start-ups launch globally every second, totaling 11,000 per hour or 25,9200 per day? Over the past decade, India has emerged as one of the world’s most dynamic start-up hubs. With more than 92,000 start-ups currently registered, India ranks among the top three most vibrant start-up ecosystems globally. The forecasted growth to over 2,00,000 start-ups by 2030 is a testament to the country’s rapidly expanding entrepreneurial network. This growth points toward the incredible opportunities and challenges within the start-up ecosystems, making it crucial to understand the fundamentals of this nurturing sector."

(Reflection : Reflect on a startup you admire. What do you think made it successful? Was it the product, the team, or the ability to pivot and adapt to market demands? Startup Terms to Know

These are the terms that show up in almost every real business conversation whether you're building something, evaluating an idea, or working inside a company. The difference is not in knowing the definitions, but in how quickly and clearly you can use them to think and make decisions.


Term
Definition

ROI (Return on Investment)

Measures how profitable an investment is relative to its cost

CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost)

Cost incurred to acquire one customer

LTV / CLTV (Customer Lifetime Value)

Total revenue expected from a customer over their lifetime

MVP (Minimum Viable Product)

Basic version of a product with minimum features to test demand

ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue)

Yearly revenue from subscriptions

MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue)

Monthly revenue from subscriptions

GMV (Gross Merchandise Value)

Total value of goods sold on a platform

Burn Rate

Rate at which a startup is spending money

Runway

Time a startup can survive before running out of cash

EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, Amortization)

Measure of operational profitability

KPI (Key Performance Indicator)

Metrics used to track business performance

Churn Rate

Percentage of customers who stop using a product

ARPU (Average Revenue Per User)

Revenue generated per user

Conversion Rate

% of users who take a desired action (e.g., sign up, buy)

TAM (Total Addressable Market)

Total market demand for a product/service

SAM (Serviceable Available Market)

Portion of TAM that you can target

SOM (Serviceable Obtainable Market)

Realistic share of the market you can capture

Equity

Ownership in a company

Valuation

Estimated worth of a company

Dilution

Reduction in ownership percentage after new investment

Vesting

Process by which founders/employees earn equity over time

Exit

Event where investors/founders cash out (e.g., acquisition, IPO)

IPO (Initial Public Offering)

When a company goes public and sells shares

Pivot

Changing business strategy based on feedback or failure

PMF (Product-Market Fit)

When a product successfully meets market demand

Basic AI

Did you know that tools powered by Artificial Intelligence can now complete tasks like research, content creation, and analysis in minutes which once took hours or even days? More importantly, individuals who effectively use AI are able to operate with significantly higher speed, clarity, and leverage.

Before you begin, here's a note from Varun, Co-Founder, Mesa:



Play Video




Think back to the last time you used an AI tool, whether to write something, brainstorm ideas, or solve a problem faster. Did it change how you approached the task? Did it make you feel more efficient, or even more confident in your output? That shift is exactly what learning to build with AI enables.

AI is no longer just a tool you occasionally use. It is becoming a fundamental part of how problems are solved, decisions are made, and products are built. In today’s world, the advantage lies not in simply knowing that AI exists, but in knowing how to apply it meaningfully.

As we define it in this context:
Building with AI is the process of using intelligent systems to enhance thinking, automate workflows, and create scalable solutions that would otherwise require significantly more time, effort, or resources.

Reflection

Think of a recent situation where you could have used AI to save time or improve your output, whether in research, writing, analysis, or communication.

What would you have done differently?

Where could AI have created the most leverage?

Objectives

By the end of this module, you will be able to:



Understand how AI is transforming the way startups build, operate, and scale

Think of AI not just as a tool, but as a core part of problem-solving

Identify opportunities where AI can create leverage in your daily work

Start using AI in a practical, hands-on way from Day 0

Build a mindset of working alongside AI, not around it

At Mesa, this is not treated as a separate skill, but as a way of operating. From Day 1, you will work hands-on with multiple tools, build practical workflows, and apply AI to real problems.

By the end of this journey, the goal is simple: you should be able to use AI to build, automate, and solve with confidence.

The earlier you start developing this mindset, the more it compounds over time.

Before we deep dive into how AI works, here are few keywords that you should get familiar with first:

Term

What it actually means

Chatbot

A chatbot is where you interact with AI using normal language. You type what you want, and it responds. It removes the need to learn code or complex tools—conversation becomes the interface.

LLM (Large Language Model)

The core system behind most AI tools. It has learned patterns from massive amounts of text and uses that to generate responses. It doesn’t “know” things like a human—it predicts what is most likely to be useful based on your input data.

Prompt

The instruction or input you give to AI. The clearer and more structured your prompt, the better the output. This is one of the most important practical skills when working with AI.

API (Application Programming Interface)

A way for different software systems to communicate. In AI, APIs let you integrate AI into apps, websites, or workflows so tasks can happen automatically without manual input every time.

Automation

Setting up systems where tasks run on their own. With AI, this could mean generating reports, replying to messages, sorting data, or triggering workflows—reducing repetitive work.

Fine-tuning / Customization

Adjusting AI to behave in a specific way. This could mean training it on your data, aligning it with your tone, or making it better suited for a particular use case instead of general output.

Multimodal AI

AI that can handle multiple types of input—text, images, audio, sometimes video. It expands what you can do beyond just writing or text-based tasks.

Hallucination

When AI generates an answer that sounds correct but isn’t factually accurate. It’s a limitation of how these systems work, which is why verification is important when using AI outputs.


Watch this video covering core concepts in AI tools and prompting techniques. It includes types of AI tools, how to surface implied context, prompting methods like zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought, along with key limitations of AI:

Play Video

Mental Exercise:

“List 3 things in your current life where AI can save your time this week.”

Here are some AI Agents made by Mesa students:

1. Invoice processing agent : WATCH HERE

This project automates manual invoice processing, a common challenge in finance teams where invoices arrive in unstructured formats via email. The system captures attachments through a Gmail trigger, validates key fields, and uses OCR and AI to extract and structure data like line items, taxes, and totals. The cleaned data is then stored in Google Sheets with unique invoice IDs to prevent duplication. By reducing manual effort and improving accuracy, it showcases how Artificial Intelligence can be applied to streamline real operational workflows.

2. Category manager - decision engine : WATCH HERE

As a category manager for fresh, this engine runs every morning and turns scattered data into a simple action list. It combines forecast, inventory, margin, and quality data to show where action is needed most. It flags key risks like overstock, stockouts, and quality issues using signals like near-expiry items and complaints. For each SKU, it suggests one clear action such as adjusting orders or applying markdowns. The top priorities are shared in a daily email, helping you act faster, reduce waste, and protect margins.

Three Claude courses to move from understanding AI to actually using it


These courses are designed to build progressively. Starting with fundamentals and moving toward real-world application and automation. No matter your background, you can follow along and apply what you learn immediately.

1. AI Fluency for Students
https://anthropic.skilljar.com/ai-fluency-for-students
Start here to build your foundation. This course helps you understand how to think with AI: from structuring prompts to approaching problems more effectively. Once you get this right, you move from vague inputs to consistently useful outputs, and everything else becomes faster and more intuitive.

2. Introduction to Claude Cowork
https://anthropic.skilljar.com/introduction-to-claude-cowork
This is where AI becomes practical. You’ll learn how to use it for real tasks—working with documents, research, notes, and multi-step workflows. It helps you turn messy information into structured outputs and start treating AI like a reliable co-worker rather than just a tool.

3. Introduction to Agent skills
https://anthropic.skilljar.com/introduction-to-agent-skills
This is where leverage kicks in. You’ll learn to create reusable instructions so AI can perform tasks consistently without repeated input. It enables you to automate repetitive work, build simple systems, and shift from using AI to setting AI up to work for you.

Community

Basic Marketing

Did you know that 53% of consumers use at least one promotional product every week, and 89% remember the brand associated with it? This demonstrates the power of effective marketing in shaping consumer behavior and boosting brand recognition.

Think back to the last time you saw an influencer showcasing a product, and you instantly felt the urge to try it. Did you save up money or at least wish you could get your hands on it sooner? That’s the power of marketing at work.

1. The 3 Financial Statements

2. Sources of Finance – Debt vs. Equity, Bonds, Stocks, Convertibles

Differences between Debt and Equity Financing

Debt and equity are the two primary ways businesses raise capital, but they operate very differently.

Debt financing:  involves borrowing money that must be repaid over time with interest. This could be in the form of bank loans, bonds, or other credit instruments. The key benefit of debt is that the business retains full ownership — lenders don’t get a stake in the company. However, debt creates a fixed financial obligation, and failure to meet repayments can lead to penalties or even bankruptcy. On the upside, interest payments are tax-deductible, reducing the effective cost of borrowing.

Equity financing: on the other hand, means raising money by selling ownership shares of the company to investors. These investors then become shareholders. There's no obligation to repay them, and there are no interest costs — which makes it a good option for companies with unpredictable cash flows or those in early stages of growth. However, equity dilutes ownership, and future profits must be shared with the new shareholders. It also means giving up some control in business decisions.

Choosing between debt and equity depends on a company’s growth stage, risk profile, cash flow stability, and appetite for control.

Understanding Bonds, Stocks, and Convertible Securities

Bonds

Bonds are a form of debt instrument where a business (or government) borrows money from investors and agrees to pay them back with interest over a fixed term. Investors receive regular interest payments (called coupon payments) and the principal back at maturity. Bonds are considered relatively safe investments, but come with risks like interest rate changes and credit default.

Stocks

Stocks represent ownership in a company. When a business issues stocks, it sells a piece of itself in exchange for funding. Investors who buy stocks become shareholders and benefit when the company grows, through price appreciation or dividends. There are two main types: common stock, which offers voting rights and variable returns, and preferred stock, which usually doesn’t come with voting rights but offers fixed dividends and priority during liquidation.

Convertible Securities

Convertible securities are hybrid instruments — they start as debt (like bonds or preference shares) but give the investor the option to convert into equity later. This gives the investor downside protection (like a bond) and upside potential (like a stock) if the company performs well. They are particularly popular in early-stage startups where future valuation growth is expected.

3. How Businesses Raise Capital Through Various Funding Sources

Businesses can raise capital through a combination of internal and external sources, each suited to different stages and needs.

Internal sources include retained earnings (profits not distributed as dividends), selling idle assets, or optimizing working capital. These are cost-effective but limited in scope.

External sources are more diverse:

Debt-based: Includes bank loans, corporate bonds, overdrafts, trade credit, and venture debt. Suitable for stable businesses with predictable income streams.

Equity-based: Includes angel investments, venture capital, private equity, and public market offerings like IPOs. Ideal for high-growth companies or startups willing to share ownership for scale.

Hybrid instruments: Include convertibles, mezzanine financing, or preference shares. These offer a mix of debt-like and equity-like features, often used to balance risk and return.

Alternative funding: Includes crowdfunding, revenue-based financing, or grants. These are useful for niche markets, early-stage startups, or companies looking for creative capital options.

Resource: Types of Business Financing - YouTube

4. Capital Budgeting – NPV, IRR, Payback Period

Net Present Value (NPV): 

Net Present Value (NPV) is a financial metric used to assess the profitability of an investment by comparing the present value of expected cash inflows to the initial investment. It discounts future cash flows to their present value using a predetermined discount rate, typically the company's cost of capital.



           Interpretation:

If NPV > 0, the investment is profitable.

If NPV = 0, the investment breaks even.

If NPV < 0, the investment is not worth pursuing.

Internal Rate of Return (IRR): 

The Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is the discount rate at which the Net Present Value (NPV) of an investment equals zero. It represents the annualized return expected from an investment and is often used to compare multiple investment opportunities.




IRR is found by trial and error or using financial calculators/software.

Interpretation:

 If IRR > cost of capital, the investment is considered profitable.

If IRR < cost of capital, the investment may not be worthwhile.

Higher IRR indicates a more attractive investment.

Payback Period: 

The payback period is the time required to recover the initial investment from the generated cash flows. It is a simple and intuitive measure of investment risk.

Formula:
PaybackPeriod=InitialInvestmentAnnualCashInflowPayback Period = \frac{Initial Investment}{Annual Cash Inflow}PaybackPeriod=AnnualCashInflowInitialInvestment​
(for projects with constant cash inflows) 


Interpretation:

A shorter payback period is preferred as it means quicker recovery of the investment.

It does not consider the time value of money, unlike NPV and IRR.

It is best used for quick assessments rather than detailed profitability analysis.

items.card: NOTE
items.text:
Effective reading, summarising, and building a POV

As you begin your journey at Mesa, one of the most important shifts you will experience is not just the volume of content, but the way you are expected to engage with it.

In a startup environment, reading is not a passive activity. Founders and operators are constantly learning through articles, reports, case studies, and market insights. Whether it is understanding a new sector, analyzing a competitor, or spotting an emerging trend, your ability to read and make sense of information directly impacts the quality of your decisions.

This means the goal is not to read more. The goal is to read better.

Objectives

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Identify key ideas, arguments, and insights in business articles and startup content

Summarise complex information clearly in your own words

Form and articulate an evidence-based opinion, distinguishing fact from interpretation

Read with intent as a founder, not just as a student

Build a system to retain, connect, and apply what you learn

Think about the last business article or report you came across. Did you read it end-to-end, or skim through it? Did you question the author’s assumptions, or accept them at face value? Did you connect it to anything you already knew?

Take a moment to reflect:

What is one thing you already do when reading?

What is one challenge you face?

It could be something like getting lost in details, struggling to identify bias, or forgetting what you read soon after. These are common, and this module is designed to help you move past them.

To set the stage, please watch/read the following:

Video (5 min): “Speed Reading Harvard Business Review – How to Read Business Cases Faster” – Paul Nowak (Iris Reading). (A quick demonstration of efficient reading strategies for dense business texts.)

Short Article: “The Art of Summarizing in Business: When, Where, and Why It Matters.” This article highlights why being able to distil complex reports into brief summaries is a valued skill in management


Key takeaway: Effective summarization shows respect for your audience’s time and proves you truly grasp the material. In fast-paced MBA classes and meetings, concise communication = credibility.

(Choose either the video or the article to start, or both if you’re curious. They illustrate why we need strong reading & summarising skills in business.)

Strategies for reading and forming opinions:

Now let’s build your toolkit for reading and summarising effectively. We’ll cover skimming, deep reading, note-taking, and opinion-forming. Start with this brief resource:

Article (8 min read): “Reading Strategies: Skimming and Scanning Techniques.” – Focus on the Skimming section for how to get the gist of an article quickly​.
Key points:

Read the title, headings, and any summary/abstract first.

Read the introductory paragraph and the first and last sentences of each paragraph​

Note bold or italicized terms (they often signal important concepts).

If something is confusing or seems important, pause and read that part fully

Skimming is great for previewing a text or reviewing it before meetings​.

A few tips & examples:

Here are some best practices to guide your reading and summarising, as described in these two articles

    Active and Critical Reading

    Summary vs Analysis

Active Reading: Don’t read passively; engage with the text. For example, make brief notes or highlights as you read – underline key sentences, jot margin notes, or use a digital highlighter. This keeps you focused and helps retention​
(Tip: try writing a one-line summary of each section or page in your own words as you go.)

Separate Facts from Opinions: As you read a business article, ask: What is the author’s thesis or main claim? What evidence is provided? Good readers constantly evaluate if the evidence is objective and credible​. Is the author trying to convince me of something? Recognize bias or assumptions by questions like: “Is the writer’s argument logical or is it based on a faulty assumption?”​

Summarizing Technique – PARAPHRASE: When you summarize, always use your own words. A summary is not copying sentences. It’s conveying the author’s ideas concisely, in a new way. This shows you truly understand the material​.

(Example: Original text: “Executives observe a drop in productivity in remote teams due to reduced in-person collaboration.” → Summary: “According to the article, working remotely can hurt productivity because people collaborate less face-to-face.”)

Forming an Opinion: After understanding the text, form your stance. Ask yourself: Do I agree with the author’s conclusions? Why or why not? Your opinion should be evidence-based – meaning it refers back to facts or points from the reading​​.

For example, if an article argues that “AI will revolutionize finance” and you’re not convinced, your opinion could be: “I’m sceptical about the claim that AI alone will revolutionise finance because the author provided only one case study of success. We need broader evidence. However, I do agree AI can streamline certain tasks (as the article’s statistics on cost savings showed).” – Here you’re citing the article’s evidence (or lack thereof) to justify your stance.

(Feel free to refer to the resource links as you digest these tips. They illustrate concepts like skimming, annotating, etc., in more detail.)

How to read and ensure you retain

One of the biggest challenges with learning at this level is retention.

You will be exposed to a large number of ideas, but without a system, most of them will fade quickly. The goal is to create a way to revisit, connect, and build on what you learn over time.

This is where tools like NotebookLM can play a role.

Instead of treating each article or lecture as a separate experience, you can bring your materials together and interact with them. You can ask questions, generate summaries, compare ideas across sources, and revisit information in different formats.

The value here is the ability to move from consuming information to synthesizing it. Over time, this helps you see patterns, identify contradictions, and develop a deeper understanding of the space you are exploring.

Play Video

Note-taking as a thinking system

If reading is the input, note-taking determines what stays with you.

Most note-taking is focused on capturing information. While this is useful, it is not enough. To truly learn, your notes need to evolve into a system that helps you think.

A helpful way to approach this is to think in layers.

The first layer is simply capturing what happened, whether it is a lecture, a discussion, or an article. The second layer is synthesis, where you identify what actually mattered. The third layer is interpretation, where you reflect on what it means and how it connects to your thinking.

Tools like Granola can support the first two layers by recording, transcribing, and organizing information. This allows you to stay present during discussions instead of trying to capture everything manually.

However, the third layer is where real learning happens. This is where you question, connect, and build your own perspective.

Over time, as you revisit your notes and combine them with new inputs, isolated pieces of information begin to form a coherent understanding.

Bringing it together

What you are building through this process is a system for learning as a founder.

AI can help you manage scale, organize content, and reduce repetitive effort. But the real value comes from how you use that support to think better.

Your role is to decide what matters, connect ideas across domains, and form clear, independent judgments.

In a startup environment, this ability compounds quickly. The better you get at learning from the world around you, the better you become at navigating uncertainty, spotting opportunities, and making decisions.

Before we wrap up, try reading the Indus valley Annual Report attached herein and see for yourself the progress you’ve made in dealing with your reading and synthesising.

items.text:
Activity
Step 1: Read with intent

Read the article: Twelve ‘why not’, ‘post-agentic AI’ Indian e-commerce scenarios from 2028

As you begin, avoid going line by line immediately. First, scan the structure. Notice how the article is organized into scenarios. Pay attention to the central theme of AI agents and how they interact with platforms, users, and businesses.

Then read in detail. As you go, try to identify patterns across scenarios rather than treating each one in isolation. 

Step 2: Identify the core Idea

Once you’ve read the piece, pause and ask yourself:

What is the central argument or thesis of this article?

What is changing in the ecosystem because of AI agents?

Which assumptions about current startups or platforms are being challenged?

Focus on understanding the big shift, not just the individual examples. 

Step 3: Synthesize the scenarios

Instead of summarizing all 12 scenarios, distill them.

Write a short summary in 4 to 5 sentences that answers:

What kind of future is the author imagining?

What happens to aggregators, marketplaces, and platforms in this world?

What role do AI agents play in decision-making and transactions?

Think of this as explaining the article to someone who has not read it.

Step 4: Form Your perspective

Now move beyond the article.

In 2 to 3 sentences, respond to the following:

Which one scenario felt most realistic or interesting to you, and why?

Do you agree with the direction the article suggests?

If you were building a startup today, how would this change your approach?

This is where you move from understanding to judgment.

Step 5: Think like a founder

Take one layer deeper.

Reflect briefly:

In a world where AI agents reduce discovery and comparison to zero, where does value shift?

What kind of startups become stronger? Which ones become fragile?

You do not need perfect answers. The goal is to start asking better questions.

Submission

Post the following in the WhatsApp group:

Your 4 to 5 sentence summary

Your perspective (2 to 3 sentences)

One insight or question that stayed with you after reading
